blogs.title: Strict Means Textual: No Signature Required to ‘Certify’ Under Louisiana’s Premium-Finance Cancellation Statute
blogs.description: The Fifth Circuit holds that La. Rev. Stat. § 9:3550(G)(3) does not require a human signature to satisfy the statute’s demand that a premium finance company “certify” specified facts before an insurer cancels for nonpayment. Reading the statute’s text against Louisiana appellate cases like Benitez, the panel emphasizes that “strict adherence” does not allow courts to add steps the legislature didn’t include. We unpack the opinion’s company-level conception of certification (as opposed to named-employee attestation), its reconciliation with prior dicta noting missing signatures, and the compliance implications for insurers and finance companies that rely on automated systems and templated certifications.

blogs.title: Receipt by Robot: Automated E‑Mail Triggers Valid Policy Cancellation in the Fifth Circuit
blogs.description: What counts as “receipt” of a cancellation request? The court leans on contemporary definitions and holds that GoAuto’s computer system “receives” APAC’s emailed certification when a web service ingests it—no human involvement necessary. We analyze how this Erie guess aligns with UETA/ESIGN-era business practices, why it matters for pinpointing the exact cancellation moment, and how it may influence other Louisiana statutes that hinge on “receipt.” The post also flags consumer-protection and litigation risks from midnight, machine-driven cancellations, and offers operational takeaways for audit trails and time-stamping.

blogs.title: The Road Not Taken: The District Court’s ‘Private Carrier’ Theory—and Why the Fifth Circuit Passed
blogs.description: The district court suggested an APAC employee hand-delivering notices fit the statute’s “private carrier” language; the Fifth Circuit called the move “imaginative and unconventional” and resolved the case on email receipt instead. We examine the structure of § 9:3550(G)(3), the risks of stretching “private carrier” to cover intrarelated-entity couriers, and how a future record without reliable electronic receipt could force courts to define that term. The piece offers counsel a roadmap for documenting delivery chains and preserving alternative theories while avoiding overbroad readings that could unsettle cancellation timing and priority-of-notice disputes.

blogs.title: No Trip to Royal Street: Fifth Circuit Declines Certification to the Louisiana Supreme Court
blogs.description: Applying its usual reluctance to certify absent a compelling reason, the Fifth Circuit refused to send unresolved questions about “receipt” and “certifying” to the Louisiana Supreme Court. We situate the move within Jefferson v. Lead Industries and the court’s Erie posture, consider the likelihood of divergent Louisiana intermediate appellate decisions post-Williams, and assess forum-selection and timing strategies for litigants. The post closes with a legislative note: if Baton Rouge wants signatures, human review, or longer cure periods in an age of automation, it must say so expressly.
